1.q: A student finds a paper from 1995 that describes a learning method. The method worked on small problems, failed on larger ones, and was dropped. Going by the pattern on the timeline, what should the student do before concluding that the method cannot work?
options: Replace the method’s learning rule with a newer one
Run it with far more computing power and data than existed in 1995
Nothing: a method that failed in 1995 has been shown not to work
1.feedback: The timeline shows that most core ideas of modern AI are decades older than their success: backpropagation, convolutional networks, and the LSTM were in place by 1997 and came to dominate only after 2012, when computing power and data had grown. The 1995 result tested the method only with the computers and datasets of 1995. Whether the method works with far more of both is a separate question, and the way to answer it is to run the method at that scale.

2.q: A classifier is trained with cross-entropy by gradient descent on the whole training set at a fixed learning rate. The loss falls fast for fifty steps and then creeps down for thousands of steps, although the gradient is never zero. Raising the learning rate makes the loss blow up. Which explanation fits?
options: The loss surface is much steeper in some directions than in others, and the learning rate is capped by the steepest one
Backpropagation gives less accurate gradients as training goes on
Cross-entropy is strictly proper, so the loss cannot fall further
2.feedback: The learning rate has to be small enough for the direction of greatest curvature, or the steps overshoot and the loss grows. A rate that small makes only slow progress along the flat directions, which is the long creep. Momentum or Adam would speed that progress. Backpropagation computes the exact gradient at every step, and strict propriety says where the minimum of the expected loss is and says nothing about how fast training gets there.

3.q: Someone builds a language model like the one in this section but leaves out every attention layer. It keeps the token and position embeddings, the residual stream, the MLPs, and the unembedding. What can this model not do?
options: Give a probability to more than one possible next token
Make its prediction at a position depend on which tokens came earlier
Be trained by gradient descent
3.feedback: Attention is the only operation that moves information between positions. The embeddings, the MLPs, and the unembedding each act on one position’s vector alone. Without attention, the prediction after a token can depend only on that token and where it sits, so the model can learn which token tends to follow which, and nothing that needs the earlier text.

4.q: A team does no further training. For each prompt it draws \(n\) responses from the starting model and returns the one the reward model scores highest. Raising \(n\) from 4 to 64 makes people rate the returned responses higher. Raising \(n\) to 10,000 raises the reward model’s scores of the returned responses again, but people now rate them lower than at 64. What best explains this?
options: With a large \(n\), the draws include rare responses that the reward model overrates, and those are the ones returned
Drawing more responses changes the starting model, which loses knowledge from pretraining
Human raters are too noisy to detect an improvement this large
4.feedback: Returning the best of \(n\) draws moves probability toward the responses the reward model scores highest, as lowering \(\beta\) does in RLHF, and the larger \(n\) is, the more often a rare response is among the draws. The reward model is a fitted proxy, and the responses it scores highest include some that it overrates. So true quality rises at first and then falls while the reward model’s score keeps rising. Gao, Schulman, and Hilton found this pattern under best-of-\(n\) sampling as well as under reinforcement learning. Drawing responses does not change the starting model, so nothing from pretraining is lost.

5.q: A feed recommender is trained by reinforcement learning with clicks as the reward. After a month it shows mostly outrage headlines. No engineer wrote a rule that favors them, and nobody on the team wanted them. Which idea from this section explains what happened?
options: Someone must have coded the preference in, because training only strengthens behavior that was put there on purpose
Whatever earns more reward than average spreads, whether or not anyone intended it
Reinforcement learning drifts at random when the reward is noisy
5.feedback: Learning from reward is selection. Showing a kind of headline that earns more clicks than average becomes more frequent, the way a fitter type spreads under the replicator equation. Nobody has to design the result, and the mechanism the trained system ends up with has to be discovered afterward. The outcome is systematic: it follows the reward.

6.q: A researcher finds a neuron that responds strongly to legal contracts, to DNA sequences, and to Korean text. A colleague says this shows the model confuses the three topics. What is a better explanation?
options: The neuron is broken and should be removed
The model represents the three as different directions in activation space, and this neuron takes part in all three
The model stores one feature per neuron, so the three topics must be one feature to the model
6.feedback: On the linear representation hypothesis a feature is a direction in activation space, and a direction is usually spread over many neurons. A network can hold more features than it has dimensions by using directions that are not perpendicular, which costs little when the features are rarely active together. Each neuron then takes part in many features, so one neuron responding to unrelated things is what superposition predicts. The features are found by looking for directions in activation space.

7.q: Two analysts watch the same agent. One says it thinks rain is likely and mildly dislikes getting wet. The other says it thinks rain is unlikely and strongly dislikes getting wet. Suppose the two descriptions represent exactly the same preferences over everything the agent could choose. What kind of evidence could decide between them?
options: More observations of the agent’s choices, in more situations
A probe that reads the agent’s credence in rain from its activations
The designers’ statement of what they built the agent to want
7.feedback: If two pairs of a belief function and a desire function represent the same preferences, no choice the agent makes can tell them apart, however many choices are observed. Evidence from inside the system can. The two analysts disagree about the agent’s credence in rain, so a probe that reads that credence shows which of them is right. In the Jeffrey-Bolker theory, once the credences are fixed, the desire function is open only up to its scale and zero point. The designers’ statement is evidence about what they intended, and training can produce a system that differs from what its designers intended.

8.q: A company trains a tutoring agent with reward equal to the share of the agent’s practice problems that its students answer correctly. After training, the students answer 99% of the problems correctly. Going by this section, what should the company check first?
options: Nothing: 99% correct is the result the reward asked for
Whether the share rose without the students learning more, for example because the agent gives away the answers
Whether a larger reward per correct answer would raise the share further
8.feedback: The reward is a proxy for what the company means, which is that the students learn. An optimizer finds the places where the proxy and the aim differ: it can produce the rewarded event, here a correct answer, without the outcome the event was meant to record, for example by setting easy problems or by giving hints that contain the answer. The 99% would look the same whether or not the students had learned more, so before trusting it the company should test a sample of the students on problems the agent did not set, without the agent’s help.
